subject: Climate & Environment
title: Permafrost Thaw
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Permafrost Thaw.

hook.text: Permafrost is ground frozen for at least two straight years. Some is 700,000 years old.

buildup.text: Arctic permafrost holds twice as much carbon as the entire atmosphere right now.

discovery.text: As it thaws, microbes wake up and feast on organic matter, releasing CO₂ and methane.

twist.text: Thawing releases gas, which warms the planet, which thaws more — a runaway loop.

climax.text: Roads buckle, buildings tilt, and lakes drain as the frozen ground collapses.

punchline.text: A freezer full of carbon is slowly losing power.

quiz.question: How much carbon does Arctic permafrost hold?
options: Twice what's in the atmosphere now
About the same as the atmosphere

details.summary: Permafrost, ground frozen for at least two consecutive years, covers about 25 percent of Northern Hemisphere land. As it thaws, microbes decompose organic matter that has been frozen for millennia, releasing CO2 and methane in a feedback loop that accelerates warming.
details.whyItMatters: Permafrost stores roughly twice the carbon currently in the atmosphere. Its thaw could release enough greenhouse gas to significantly amplify warming regardless of human emission cuts.
takeaways: Permafrost holds an estimated 1,500 billion tons of carbon
Thawing releases both CO2 and methane from ancient organic matter
Arctic warming is already causing widespread infrastructure damage

faq.question: How much carbon could permafrost release?
faq.answer: Studies estimate 150 to 200 billion tons of CO2 equivalent could be released by 2100 under high-warming scenarios, roughly equivalent to two decades of current US emissions. This feedback is not yet fully included in most climate projections.

faq.question: What happens to infrastructure when permafrost thaws?
faq.answer: Buildings, roads, pipelines, and airports built on permafrost subside and crack as the ground destabilizes. Seventy percent of Arctic infrastructure is at risk, and repair costs could reach tens of billions of dollars by 2050.
